hook.text: Give three models the same two hundred points, and each one draws a different border. Logistic regression draws a straight line. A decision tree cuts in steps. Nearest neighbors bends with the data. On points they haven't seen, they score eighty-two, eighty-nine and ninety-three percent.

plan.text: The model round asks how each one draws its border, and when you'd pick it. Of the fifteen questions here, eleven get a model fitted on screen, and four get a sentence each at the end.

logit.text: Question one. What is logistic regression, and how does it output probabilities? It adds up the features into a score, the log odds, then passes that score through the sigmoid, which squeezes any number into the range zero to one.

logit-fit.text: Here are five hundred sixty-nine tumors, and one feature: the mean radius of their cells. The score is minus fifteen point two five, plus one point oh three for each unit of radius. At a radius of fifteen, the score is point two six, and the sigmoid turns it into a probability of fifty-six percent. Each extra unit multiplies the odds of malignancy by two point eight.

linear.text: Question two. Why not linear regression for a binary target? Fit a straight line to the same zeros and ones, and it leaves the range: below zero for sixty tumors, above one for thirty-five. At a radius of twenty-eight, it predicts one point seven six, which no probability can be. Logistic regression stays inside, and it's fitted by maximum likelihood.

tree-in.text: Next, the model that cuts in steps.

tree.text: Question three. How does a decision tree split? It tries every threshold on every feature, and keeps the cut that leaves the two sides purest.

tree-gini.text: Here are a hundred iris flowers, two species, half and half. Gini impurity, the chance that two flowers picked at random differ, starts at point five. Slide a cut along petal width. At one point seven five, one side is forty-nine to five, the other one to forty-five, and the weighted impurity falls to point one one, the lowest of any cut.

bag-in.text: One tree is quick to read, and quick to overreact. So, many trees.

bag.text: Question four. What's the difference between bagging and boosting? Bagging trains many models side by side, each on a bootstrap sample, rows drawn with replacement, and averages them. One deep tree on this noisy sine wave chases every point. Two hundred bagged trees average the noise out, and test error falls from point two six to point one eight. Bagging cuts variance.

boost.text: Boosting trains small models one after another, each fitted to what the ones before it still get wrong. After one tree the fit is crude, after ten it's close, and after a hundred, test error is point one seven five. Boosting cuts bias. It's often the more accurate of the two, but it can overfit noisy data, where bagging holds up.

forest.text: Question five. How does a random forest work? It's bagged trees with one more twist: at every split, a tree may only look at a random handful of features, here five of thirty. The trees stop all making the same cuts, so their mistakes overlap less, and the average gains more. On a hundred seventy-one held-out tumors, one tree scores ninety point six percent, bagged trees ninety-three, and the forest ninety-five point three.

ada.text: Question six. How does gradient boosting differ from AdaBoost?

knn-in.text: Back to the border that bent with the data.

knn.text: Question seven. How does k-nearest neighbors, or KNN, make predictions? It keeps every training point. For a new one, it finds the k closest, and takes a vote. Here, fifteen neighbors, ten against five. There's no training step, but prediction is slow on large data.

knn-k.text: And k sets the trade-off. At k equals one, every point owns a patch of its own: a hundred percent on the training points, seventy-nine on new ones. At fifteen, the border is smooth, and scores ninety-three. At seventy-five, it's nearly straight, and drops to eighty-seven. Small k is high variance, large k high bias, so choose it by cross-validation.

kmeans-in.text: Neighbors need labels. Without them, you cluster.

kmeans.text: Question eight. What is k-means clustering? Place k centers, assign each point to the nearest one, move each center to the mean of its points, and repeat until nothing moves. These three centers all start in one group. After one move, two of them jump toward the other groups, and on the third pass, it settles.

kmeans-k.text: It minimizes the within-cluster sum of squares, which always falls as k grows, so look for the elbow. Here it drops from twenty thousand at one cluster to five sixty-seven at three, then barely moves. The silhouette score, how much nearer each point sits to its own cluster than to the next, peaks at three as well.

pca-in.text: More features bring trouble of their own.

pca.text: Question nine. What is PCA? Principal component analysis finds the directions in which the data varies most, each at right angles to the last, and projects the data onto the first few. On the four iris measurements, scaled first, one component holds seventy-three percent of the variance, and two hold ninety-six. Four columns become two, and the species still separate. It needs centered data, and it only finds straight-line structure.

curse.text: Question ten. What is the curse of dimensionality? As dimensions grow, space empties out. Scatter a thousand random points. In two dimensions, a point's nearest neighbor is about sixty times closer than its farthest. In a thousand dimensions, the nearest is almost as far as the farthest. Distances stop telling points apart, and KNN and k-means suffer first. The fixes: fewer dimensions, through PCA or feature selection, and regularization.

shap-in.text: The last deep dive: which features mattered.

shap.text: Question eleven. What's the difference between a forest's built-in feature importance and SHAP values, short for Shapley additive explanations? The built-in one adds up how much each feature cut impurity, across every tree. It's fast, but it favors features with many distinct values.

shap-id.text: Here's a made-up churn table, with a customer ID that means nothing at all. Impurity importance gives the ID forty percent, four times the plan, which really does drive churn.

shap-values.text: SHAP splits each prediction fairly among the features, using game theory. This customer starts from the average, point five oh. The monthly plan adds point one eight, fifty-six months of tenure takes away point two two, and the other two bring it to point four seven five. Averaged over customers, SHAP ranks the plan first and the ID last.

rapid-in.text: The last four are quicker, and three of them are about the inputs rather than the model.

r-gen.text: A discriminative model learns the probability of the label given the input, like logistic regression. A generative model learns how the inputs are spread within each class, like naive Bayes, then classifies with Bayes' theorem. It can generate data, and it copes better with few labels.

r-scale.text: Scale features for anything built on distances or gradient descent: KNN, k-means, support vector machines and linear models. On the wine data, KNN goes from sixty-nine percent to ninety-five once the features are standardized. A tree scores eighty-nine either way.

r-encode.text: One-hot encoding gives each category its own column of zeros and ones. Ordinal encoding maps ordered categories to integers. Target encoding uses each category's mean outcome, which leaks unless it's computed inside cross-validation.

r-select.text: And feature selection comes in three kinds. Filters score each feature on its own. Wrappers, like recursive feature elimination, try subsets with a model. Embedded methods select while training, like the lasso. Here, recursive elimination keeps five of the thirty tumor features.

next.text: Every model here is built from parts you can point to: a line, a cut, a distance. A neural network learns its own. Next: deep learning.

tree-stop.text: Then the tree repeats this on each side, until a stopping rule, like a maximum depth.

gb.text: Gradient boosting fits each new tree to the negative gradient of the loss, called the pseudo-residuals. For squared error, they're just the residuals, but any differentiable loss will do.

adaboost.text: AdaBoost, short for adaptive boosting, re-weights the data instead: after every round, the points it got wrong count for more. After three rounds, this point carries thirty-five times the weight of the easiest ones. AdaBoost turns out to be gradient boosting with an exponential loss.

kmeans-starts.text: And run several starts, or k-means plus plus, because a bad start can settle in the wrong place.

tree-measures.text: Entropy, the measure behind information gain, picks the same cut here. A regression tree picks the cut that shrinks the variance most.

kmeans-limits.text: It assumes round clusters of similar size, and outliers drag the means toward them.

shap-perm.text: It still gives the ID thirteen percent, because SHAP explains the model, and this forest does use the ID. To ask whether a feature helps on new customers, shuffle it on held-out rows and measure how much accuracy drops. That's permutation importance, and it gives the ID seven percent, the plan fifty-three.
